# Data in BiologyToBioimage: everything is generated by code

The repository stores **no data files and no pictures**. Every image, time-lapse, point pattern
and figure in the 37 notebooks is produced by code that runs inside the notebook. Data come from
the simulators in [`course_toolkit.py`](course_toolkit.py) (copied verbatim into each notebook that
uses them) or from small simulation functions written in the notebook itself.

Why simulate?

- **A known truth.** Every simulator returns the hidden ground truth — the true cell shapes and
  positions, the true association between two channels, the true lineage of a dividing cell, the
  true transform relating two images — so every method can be *checked*: the notebooks contain
  🧪 *ground-truth checks* that a real, unlabelled microscopy image could not provide.
- **A slim, self-contained repository.** Nothing to download, no licences to track, no broken
  links; every notebook runs offline on a free CPU in minutes.
- **Reproducible.** A fixed `SEED` means every notebook (and every student) sees the same data and
  the same numbers.

What simulation cannot teach — the messiness, scale and artefacts of real microscopy data — is
covered in each Level 2 module's 🧭 *From toy to real data* section, which names public tools,
model zoos and landmark data sets to try next. The synthetic images reproduce the *structure* of
real bioimages (blobby or elongated objects, point-spread-function blur, sensor and shot noise,
multiple channels, time); they never claim to reproduce a specific published data set, and the
notebooks say so.

---

## Core simulators (`course_toolkit.py`)

| Simulator | Mimics | What it returns (hidden truth in **bold**) | Modules |
|---|---|---|---|
| `simulate_nuclei_image(...)` | a fluorescence image of cell nuclei/cells (round, elongated, kidney-shaped, …), optionally touching or dividing | the image, **instance mask**, **shape class per cell**, **cell centres/radii** | 00, 02, 13–21, 27–30, 32, 34 |
| `simulate_two_channel_image(...)` | two co-imaged fluorescence channels (e.g. two labelled proteins) with a chosen degree of spatial association | both channel images, **the planted association strength**, **per-spot ground truth** | 13, 26, 29, 36 |
| `simulate_time_lapse(...)` | a time-lapse of moving, occasionally dividing particles or cells | the frame sequence, **per-object trajectories**, **division events/lineage** | 22, 36 |
| `simulate_point_pattern(...)` | a 2-D spatial point pattern (e.g. molecule or cell positions) | the coordinates, **the planted pattern**: random / clustered / dispersed | 13, 26 |
| `simulate_registration_pair(...)` | a "moving" image obtained by applying a known rigid/similarity transform to a reference image | both images, **the true transform** (rotation, translation, scale) | 23 |
| `degrade_image(image, psf_sigma, noise_sigma, seed)` | the forward imaging model: blur by a known point-spread function plus sensor noise | the degraded image, **the true PSF and noise level used to generate it** | 24, 25, 28, 29 |
| `gaussian_psf(sigma, radius)`, `blur_image(image, psf)` | the microscope's optical blur (point-spread function) and convolving an image with it | the PSF kernel / the blurred image | 02, 12, 24, 25 |
| `add_gaussian_noise`, `add_poisson_noise`, `add_salt_pepper_noise`, `add_periodic_noise` | the classic noise sources of a camera sensor: read noise, shot noise, impulse noise, scan-line pickup | the noisy image (clean image kept for comparison) | 02, 24 |

## Physics/instrumentation simulators (`course_toolkit.py`, Modules 03–10)

These model the microscope itself — optics, light, and the detector — rather than a biological
specimen; several extend `simulate_nuclei_image`'s synthetic cells as the specimen being imaged.

| Simulator | Mimics | What it returns (hidden truth in **bold**) | Modules |
|---|---|---|---|
| `thin_lens_image_distance`, `ray_transfer_free_space`, `ray_transfer_thin_lens`, `trace_rays_through_system` | the thin-lens equation and ABCD paraxial ray tracing through a lens system | the image distance / a traced ray's height and angle at each surface, from **known** lens parameters | 03 |
| `numerical_aperture`, `rayleigh_resolution`, `abbe_resolution` | an objective's light-gathering power and the diffraction-limited resolution it sets | NA, and the Rayleigh/Abbe resolution limit, from **known** wavelength and NA | 03, 04 |
| `simulate_psf`, `zernike_radial`, `zernike` | Fourier-optics PSF formation from a circular aperture, optionally with a Zernike-polynomial wavefront aberration | the simulated PSF image, from a **known**, exactly specified pupil/aberration | 04, 05 |
| `make_phase_object`, `zernike_phase_contrast`, `dic_shear_render` | a weak-phase object and the bright-field/dark-field/phase-contrast/DIC images a microscope would form of it | each contrast mode's rendered image, from the **same known** underlying phase object | 06 |
| `fluorophore_spectrum`, `dichroic_transmission` | a fluorophore's Gaussian excitation/emission spectra and a dichroic/filter's logistic transmission curve | the spectral curves and the resulting bleed-through integral, from **known** peak wavelengths and cutoffs | 07 |
| `confocal_optical_section`, `two_photon_vs_one_photon_profile`, `tirf_evanescent_intensity` | axial (z) response of confocal pinhole sectioning, one- vs. two-photon excitation, and TIRF's evanescent decay | the axial intensity profile, from a **known** optical model (no real z-stack) | 08 |
| `simulate_storm_acquisition`, `gaussian_psf`, `add_gaussian_noise`, `blur_image`, `fit_gaussian_spot` | sparse, stochastic single-molecule blinking and per-blink Gaussian-centroid localisation (STORM/PALM) | the raw blinking movie and **the true emitter positions** each blink is localised against | 08 |
| `sensor_noise_model`, `quantize_bits` | the full camera detection chain (QE, dark current, read noise, gain) and bit-depth quantization | the simulated noisy, quantized image, from a **known** photon count | 09 |
| `photobleaching_curve`, `photon_budget_tradeoff` | photobleaching as a function of cumulative dose, and the SNR-vs-photons-per-frame trade-off | the remaining-fluorescence curve / the SNR curve, from **known** bleaching and photon-budget parameters | 09, 10 |
| `simulate_uneven_illumination`, `flat_field_correct` | vignetting/uneven illumination and the flat-field shading correction that removes it | the shaded image and the corrected image, checked against the **known, planted** illumination field | 10 |

## Worked-example tables (toolkit constants)

| Constant | What it is | Modules |
|---|---|---|
| `SHAPE_CLASSES` | the fixed set of synthetic nucleus/cell shape classes (`_draw_blob` draws one) used throughout the course as the classification/segmentation/tracking target | 13, 15–21, 27–30, 32, 34 |
| `SOBEL_X`, `SOBEL_Y` | the literal 3×3 Sobel gradient kernels | 14 |

## Simulators written locally in a single notebook

Several modules — mostly in Level 2, where no one shared simulator fits every research area —
define a small, documented simulator of their own rather than adding it to the shared toolkit (the
rule in *Rules for contributors* below explains why):

| Local simulator (where it is defined) | Mimics | Hidden truth |
|---|---|---|
| A textured "speckle" image pair under a known flow field (Module 22) | a speckled/textured tissue or bead-seeded gel sheared or flowing between two frames, for validating Lucas-Kanade optical flow | **the true analytic flow field `(v_y, v_x)` applied to warp frame 0 into frame 1** |
| In-/out-of-distribution shape-mix evaluation sets (Module 28) | a held-out shape mixture the model was not tuned on, to compare a specialist U-Net against a training-free generalist segmenter | **which shapes are in- vs. out-of-distribution** |
| Paired label-free/"stained" channel pairs (Module 29) | a low-contrast, blurred "label-free" view paired with a crisp "ground-truth stain" view of the same cells | **the true stain intensity the model must predict, and when it is forced to hallucinate** |
| Per-treatment cell populations with an injected batch effect (Module 30) | a high-content screen across simulated treatments and plates/batches | **the true treatment effect**, separated from **the injected, purely technical batch effect** |
| A multiplexed, multi-marker synthetic tissue (Module 31) | several co-imaged marker channels defining a handful of synthetic cell types arranged with planted spatial structure | **per-cell type**, **the planted spatial neighbourhood structure/niches** |
| A calibration/active-learning classifier pool (Module 32) | a pool of labelled and unlabelled synthetic cells for calibration and active-learning experiments | **the true label of every pool image**, used only for evaluation, never for training before it is "labelled" |
| A small 3-D nuclei volume (Module 33) | a multi-plane, correlated-in-z extension of the 2-D nucleus simulator | **the full-volume 3-D instance mask** |
| An out-of-distribution test set and a leaky vs. grouped train/test split (Module 34) | the two most common ways a bioimage model silently fails: distribution shift and data leakage | **which split is leaky**, **which test images are out of distribution** |
| A toy model-zoo registry and a synthetic text corpus (Module 35) | a BioImage.IO-style registry of tools an agent can call, and a small corpus for a retrieval demo | **the correct tool/answer for each query**, used to check the agent's and the retriever's output |

These are documented where they are defined, follow the same SIMULATED-labelling and
ground-truth-return conventions as the shared toolkit, and reuse the shared toolkit's simulators as
their building blocks wherever that is natural (for example, several extend `simulate_nuclei_image`
rather than drawing cells from scratch).

---

## Rules for contributors

- Do not add data files, pictures, downloads or file reads. The validator
  (`python validate_notebooks.py`) rejects stored data files, files over 400 kB, embedded or linked
  pictures (the Colab badge is the only external image), and code that downloads or reads data.
- Generate data with the toolkit or with a documented simulation function in the notebook; return
  the hidden truth and use it in a 🧪 ground-truth check.
- Label simulated data (print a line noting it is simulated, put "SIMULATED" in plot titles where
  natural) and explain what the simulation mimics and what it cannot teach.
- If a new simulator is useful to several notebooks, add it to `course_toolkit.py`, then replace the
  copy in the 🧰 toolkit cell of every notebook that uses it — the validator reports copies that
  differ from the reference file.
